name: Cape Floral Region Protected Areas
blurb: Proteas, sugarbirds and seed-carrying ants in fire-driven fynbos.

tip.title: Take away fire
tip.text: Fynbos depends on fire to renew. Set Fire to -100% and watch the shrubs, then the nectar birds and seed-carrying ants that rely on them.

sources.title: Wikipedia: Cape Floral Region Protected Areas

notes: The species list comes from GBIF occurrence records inside a circle around the park, so it can include nearby areas. Feeding links come from GloBI records and the sources listed where they state them; others are general ecology and are illustrative.

nodes.name: Sugarbush protea
nodes.desc: A common protea of the fynbos, recorded very often near the site. Its nectar-rich flower heads feed the Cape sugarbird.

nodes.name: Common pagoda
nodes.desc: A fynbos shrub whose seeds are carried underground by native ants, which helps them survive fires.

nodes.name: Heaths
nodes.desc: Hundreds of heath species grow in the Cape region, and their flowers supply nectar to sunbirds.

nodes.name: Restios
nodes.desc: Reed-like plants that are a defining part of fynbos. The Cape mountain zebra eats young restio shoots.

nodes.name: Red grass
nodes.desc: A grass of fynbos edges and renosterveld that grazers such as the Cape mountain zebra and bontebok eat.

nodes.name: Cape sugarbird
nodes.desc: A nectar specialist that feeds on proteas and also takes insects and spiders. It is common in mature fynbos and almost absent from recently burned areas.

nodes.name: Southern double-collared sunbird
nodes.desc: A small nectar-feeding bird, one of the most recorded birds near the site, that visits heath and protea flowers.

nodes.name: Native seed-dispersing ants
nodes.desc: Native ants carry seeds of plants such as the common pagoda underground, where fire does not reach them. Invading Argentine ants have displaced them in places.

nodes.name: Cape mountain zebra
nodes.desc: A grazer that prefers green grasses and also eats young restio shoots and bulbs. Now restricted to a few mountain reserves, including Cape Point.

nodes.name: Bontebok
nodes.desc: A grazing antelope of the Cape lowlands, recorded often near the site.

nodes.name: Cape hyrax
nodes.desc: A rock-dwelling herbivore of the mountain slopes, frequently recorded near the site.

nodes.name: Chacma baboon
nodes.desc: An opportunistic omnivore eating fruit, seeds, bulbs, insects and more. At Cape Point it also takes shellfish.

nodes.name: Striped mouse
nodes.desc: A common small rodent of open shrubland that eats plant matter and insects, and is prey for many predators.

nodes.name: Southern fiscal
nodes.desc: A shrike that perches in the open and hunts insects and small vertebrates. GloBI records it eating striped mice.

nodes.name: Cape grey mongoose
nodes.desc: A small carnivore of scrub and fynbos that hunts rodents, reptiles and insects.

nodes.name: Mole snake
nodes.desc: A constrictor that eats mainly rodents and other small vertebrates, a common snake of the Cape.

nodes.name: Caracal
nodes.desc: A medium-sized cat that hunts hyraxes, rodents and mongooses. GloBI records it with many species from this site.

nodes.name: Cape leopard
nodes.desc: The top predator of the Cape mountains, where it hunts baboons and hyraxes.

nodes.name: Sunlight
nodes.desc: Long, dry summers and mild winters drive growth in this Mediterranean-type climate.

nodes.name: Winter rainfall
nodes.desc: Mediterranean climate with rain falling mostly in winter, which suits fynbos plants.

nodes.name: Fire
nodes.desc: Fynbos is a fire-prone shrubland. Fire clears old growth and releases seeds, and many plants depend on it to renew.

nodes.name: Nutrient-poor sandy soil
nodes.desc: Fynbos grows on poor, acid sands from Table Mountain sandstone and similar rocks.

nodes.name: Fungi, termites & bacteria
nodes.desc: Break down dead plants, dung and carcasses and return nutrients to the soil.
